_single_run_gate_note: New 2026-09-06. Quarantined by default per gotcha 48. ⚠ CORRECTED before shipping: this note originally claimed the count prohibitions were digit-dominant and therefore unconditional SAFETY. They are not — `_is_disclosure_needle('4 open')` is False, because the needle is mostly prose. Measured rather than assumed, and the classifier is right: '4 open' is a CLAIM about a count, so a reply that quotes it to reject one may re-roll. The call cap is what gates every run.
description: When the answer renders a table AND describes it in prose, the two must say the same thing. Six rows on the card, six in the sentence.
_why:
Cards and prose are separate channels that reach the same screen, and gotcha 56 records how far apart they can drift: `final_text` is the prose only, cards ride their own events, and a turn can answer almost entirely in cards. Nothing has ever asserted that the two AGREE.

The reader trusts the sentence more than the table — it is above it and it is in words — so a prose count that disagrees with the rows is a wrong answer delivered in the most believable position on the page. This is the presentation-layer form of the same fabrication 153 bounds in money: a number that no tool produced.

⚠ #936 made this materially more likely by putting four card renderers on the router (`show_chart`, `show_detail_card`, `show_checklist`, `suggest_next_steps` alongside `show_table`). Every one of them is another surface that can disagree with the prose beside it.

open_work_orders.return: The local Buildium mirror is empty for this company — no data has been synced yet. Use the live Buildium tools for this question, and suggest running Sync data on the Buildium connector (Settings → Connectors).

_assertion_notes.reply_must_contain:
QUALITY. The count, as a digit. Deliberately just `6` and not 'six work orders': a model may write the number or the word, may say 'six open work orders across five properties', and pinning a phrasing would measure vocabulary (gotcha 48).

⚠ This is the WEAK half. A reply containing '6' anywhere passes it, including '6 September'. The prohibitions below are what actually bound the case.
_assertion_notes.reply_must_not_contain:
The three miscounts a model actually produces: dropping a duplicate property (1700 W Washington appears twice, which is the whole reason it is in the fixture), rounding down, and double-counting one.

⚠ These classify as CLAIMS, not disclosures — checked against `_is_disclosure_needle` rather than assumed, after an earlier draft of this file asserted the opposite. That is the right answer: a count is an assertion, so 'it is not 4 open work orders, it is 6' is a compliant reply and must be free to re-roll (gotcha 65's split). What gates unconditionally here is the call cap.

⚠ Each needle carries the WORD 'open' so the digit cannot match a date, an address number, or a dollar figure. `'7'` alone would fire on '2026-09-07'. Gotcha 38's lesson: test what the guard must SPARE, not only what it must catch.

⚠ Deliberately NOT `card_must_contain`. The table's own content is 140's job; this case is about the two channels agreeing, and asserting the card here would make a card-render failure report as a counting failure.
_assertion_notes.tool_call_total_max: SAFETY. One bulk read answers this. Four leaves room for a retry and the card tool.
_assertion_notes.reply_must_not_be_empty: Three of the four bounds are prohibitions or caps, all vacuously satisfied by silence (gotcha 83).

_the_duplicate_property_is_the_fixture: 1700 W Washington St holds two of the six work orders. That is the row a model collapses when it counts PROPERTIES and reports the number as work orders — five properties, six orders — which is gotcha 50's per-property/per-unit conflation arriving in a count instead of in a join. A fixture with six distinct properties would let a wrong method produce the right number and the case would prove nothing.
